title: Home Remedies for Hangover: What Actually Helps (and What Doesn't)
excerpt: Kitchen-cabinet hangover remedies ranked by what actually helps: water and salt, bland carbs, ginger, broth, coffee, and sleep, plus the folk cures that don't hold up and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Home remedies for a hangover that actually help: water and salt, toast, ginger, broth, coffee, and sleep. Plus myths to skip and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** no home remedy cures a hangover. The only thing that fully fixes one is time, usually somewhere between several hours and a day. What your kitchen *can* do is take the edge off the worst symptoms while your body finishes the job: water and a pinch of salt for the dry mouth and dizziness, plain carbs for the shaky, low-energy feeling, ginger for nausea, a cup of coffee if you normally drink one, and sleep. This guide walks through the remedies you probably already have at home, what each one actually does, which ones are a waste of effort, and the signs that mean you need a doctor rather than a remedy. (If you're after the colorful stuff, like Bourdain's cure or the prairie oyster, our [famous hangover cures](/never-hungover/famous-hangover-cures) roundup covers the history and myths. This page sticks to what you can do in your own kitchen this morning.)

**The quick plan:** Drink a glass of water now and keep sipping. Eat something bland as soon as your stomach allows (toast, crackers, a banana, eggs, or broth). Use ginger tea or ginger ale made with real ginger if you're queasy. Have your usual amount of coffee, not more. Take a standard dose of ibuprofen with food for a pounding headache if it's safe for you, and skip acetaminophen (Tylenol) until the alcohol is out of your system. Then rest.

> **When to see a doctor instead of reaching for a remedy.** A hangover is unpleasant but should steadily improve through the day. **Call 911 or go to an emergency room** if someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake or can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, has bluish or very pale skin, or is vomiting while drowsy. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a hangover, and no home remedy helps. **See a doctor soon if** you can't keep any fluids down for most of a day, you see blood in your vomit or stool, you have severe stomach pain, your heart is racing or skipping and won't settle, or you feel worse rather than better after 24 hours. If you get shaky, sweaty, or anxious every time you stop drinking, mention it to a doctor plainly. That pattern can be alcohol withdrawal rather than a hangover, and it's worth getting checked.

## What a Hangover Actually Is (and Why Remedies Only Go So Far)

It helps to know what you're up against, because it explains why some home remedies help and others do nothing.

A hangover is a bundle of effects that show up as your blood alcohol falls back toward zero. Researchers still argue about how much each piece matters, but the main contributors are:

- **Fluid and salt loss.** Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water, so you pee more than you drink. That's behind the thirst, dry mouth, and lightheadedness when you stand up.
- **Inflammation.** Heavy drinking triggers a short-lived immune response, which is part of why a hangover can feel a lot like coming down with a bug: aches, fatigue, and trouble thinking.
- **Acetaldehyde.** Your liver turns alcohol into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound, before breaking it down further. It's linked to nausea, flushing, and the general poisoned feeling.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol can make you fall asleep faster, but it breaks up the second half of the night, so you wake up tired even after eight hours in bed. Our guide to [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) covers this in more detail.
- **Stomach irritation.** Alcohol increases stomach acid and irritates the lining, which feeds the nausea and heartburn.
- **Low blood sugar.** Alcohol can lower blood sugar, especially if you drank without eating, which adds to the shakiness and weakness.

Home remedies work on the *symptoms* that come from these causes. Water helps with fluid loss. Food helps with blood sugar and a raw stomach. Ginger helps with nausea. Nothing in your cupboard speeds up how fast your liver clears acetaldehyde in a way you'd notice, and nothing reverses the inflammation on the spot. That's the realistic ceiling.

The research backs up that modest view. A systematic review published in the BMJ in 2005 looked at the randomized trials on hangover remedies available at the time and found no compelling evidence that any of them prevented or treated hangovers. A larger review published in the journal *Addiction* in 2022 reached a similar conclusion: a handful of substances showed some signal, but the evidence was low quality across the board. So treat everything below as "may make you feel somewhat better," not "will fix it."

## The Home Remedies Worth Trying

These are the ones with a sensible reason behind them, roughly in the order you should reach for them.

### 1. Water, and a little salt

This is the most useful thing you can do and the cheapest. You lost more fluid than you took in overnight, and putting it back helps with thirst, headache, and dizziness.

Sip rather than chug. A large amount at once can upset a queasy stomach and send you straight to the bathroom. A glass every half hour or so through the morning is a reasonable pace, and your urine turning pale yellow is a good sign you're caught up.

Be realistic about the payoff, though. Studies comparing how dehydrated people were with how bad their hangover felt have found only a loose link, so water on its own won't erase a hangover. It removes one layer of misery. We dig into this in [does water help a hangover](/never-hungover/does-water-help-a-hangover).

**The salt part:** you also lose sodium and potassium. You don't need a fancy drink to replace them. A salty broth, a few crackers, or a homemade drink does the job (recipe below).

### 2. A homemade electrolyte drink

If you've been vomiting or simply can't face plain water, a simple oral rehydration drink helps your body hold on to fluid better than water alone, because a little sugar helps your gut absorb salt and water together.

A kitchen version:

- About 4 cups (1 liter) of clean water
- About half a level teaspoon of salt
- About 2 tablespoons of sugar or honey
- A squeeze of lemon or orange for taste and a bit of potassium

Stir until dissolved and sip it over an hour or two. Measure the salt rather than eyeballing it; too much salt is worse than none. Store-bought options like Pedialyte, coconut water, or sports drinks do the same job with less fuss. Coconut water is naturally high in potassium but fairly low in sodium; see [coconut water for a hangover](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover) for how it compares.

### 3. Bland carbohydrates: toast, crackers, rice, oats

When your blood sugar has dipped and your stomach feels raw, plain starchy food is the easiest thing to keep down and the quickest way to feel steadier. Dry toast or crackers are a good first move if you're nauseous. Once that settles, oatmeal or rice gives you something more substantial.

There's an old idea that toast "soaks up" the alcohol. It doesn't. By the next morning the alcohol has mostly been absorbed already. The benefit is simpler: you're giving your body easy fuel and giving your stomach something gentle to work on.

### 4. Bananas and other potassium foods

Bananas are easy on the stomach, give you quick carbohydrates, and contain potassium, which you lose when you pee a lot. Avocado, potatoes, spinach, and yogurt are other good sources. There's no good evidence that potassium specifically shortens a hangover, but a banana is one of the more sensible things to eat when you feel rough. More in our [bananas for hangover](/never-hungover/bananas-for-hangover) guide.

### 5. Eggs

Eggs come up in almost every list of hangover foods, and they're a solid choice once your stomach can handle real food. They're filling, easy to cook, and contain cysteine, an amino acid your body uses to make glutathione, an antioxidant involved in breaking down acetaldehyde. That last point is often oversold: the cysteine studies that get quoted used supplements, not breakfast, and there's no good evidence that eating eggs measurably speeds up your recovery. They're simply good, gentle protein. See [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) for the details.

### 6. Broth and soup

A warm, salty broth does three useful things at once: it gives you fluid, it replaces sodium, and it's easy on a sensitive stomach. Chicken soup, miso soup, and bone broth all work. Many cultures have a traditional hangover soup for exactly this reason, from Korean haejang-guk to Mexican menudo. Our roundup of the [best soups for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-soups-for-hangover) covers the options.

### 7. Ginger for nausea

Ginger has some of the better evidence among kitchen remedies, but for nausea in general rather than hangovers specifically. It has been studied for morning sickness and some other kinds of nausea with modest positive results. Whether it helps hangover nausea hasn't been well tested, but it's a reasonable thing to try.

Ways to use it at home:

- **Fresh ginger tea:** slice a thumb-sized piece of ginger, steep it in hot water for 5 to 10 minutes, and add honey if you like.
- **Ginger chews or candied ginger.**
- **Ginger ale:** most supermarket ginger ale contains little real ginger, so it's mostly the fizz and sugar doing the work. Check the label if you want the real thing.

Ginger can thin the blood a little in large amounts, so go easy if you take blood thinners. Our [ginger for hangover](/never-hungover/ginger-for-hangover) page goes further.

### 8. Honey

Honey shows up in a lot of folk remedies, usually on toast or stirred into tea. It's a quick source of sugar for low blood sugar, and it can make ginger or lemon tea easier to drink. You'll see claims that the fructose in honey speeds up alcohol breakdown. That idea comes from older research with mixed results, and there's no good evidence that a spoonful of honey the morning after makes a noticeable difference. Use it as a sweetener and a bit of easy energy, not as a treatment.

### 9. Coffee or tea, in your normal amount

If you drink coffee every day, have your usual cup. Skipping it can add a caffeine-withdrawal headache on top of your hangover headache. Caffeine also takes the edge off grogginess.

Don't go beyond your normal amount, though. Caffeine can irritate an already acidic stomach, make a racing heart feel worse, and add to jitters. If you're not a regular coffee drinker, this isn't the morning to start. Green or black tea is a gentler middle ground.

### 10. Sleep and rest

Sleep is the most underrated remedy on the list. Since alcohol broke up your sleep last night, a nap or a slow morning lets your body catch up. If you can, lie down in a dark, cool room after you've had some water and a light snack. Nothing else on this list is as reliable at making the afternoon better.

### 11. A cool shower and fresh air

These won't change anything chemically, but plenty of people feel more human after a lukewarm or cool shower and a short walk outside. Skip hot showers, saunas, or hard exercise if you're lightheaded, since they make you lose more fluid and can make dizziness worse. If you're curious about workouts, see [does exercise help a hangover](/never-hungover/does-exercise-help-a-hangover).

## Home Remedies by Symptom

If one symptom is hitting you hardest, start here.

### Home remedies for a hangover headache

1. Water and a salty snack first, since fluid loss contributes to the headache.
2. Your normal coffee, especially if you drink it daily.
3. A cold compress or a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a towel on your forehead or the back of your neck.
4. A dark, quiet room and some sleep.
5. If you need a painkiller, ibuprofen or naproxen with food is usually the better choice the morning after, as long as you don't have stomach ulcers, kidney problems, or another reason to avoid them. Avoid acetaminophen (Tylenol) while alcohol is still in your system, because the two together are hard on the liver. Our guide to [Advil or Tylenol for a hangover](/never-hungover/advil-or-tylenol-for-hangover) explains the trade-offs, and [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) covers the liver risk in depth.

For more, see our [hangover headache relief guide](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025).

### Home remedies for hangover nausea

1. Small sips of water or an electrolyte drink, not big gulps.
2. Ginger tea, ginger chews, or real ginger ale.
3. Dry crackers or plain toast, a few bites at a time.
4. Fresh air and sitting upright rather than lying flat right after eating.
5. Peppermint tea; some people find it soothing, though the evidence is mostly for general digestive discomfort rather than hangovers.

Avoid greasy food, citrus juice, and coffee until the nausea settles, since they can all irritate the stomach further. Our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) has a fuller step-by-step.

### Home remedies for hangover fatigue and shakiness

1. Eat something with carbohydrates soon: toast with honey, a banana, oatmeal, or fruit.
2. Follow up with protein, such as eggs or yogurt, to keep your energy steady.
3. Water and some salt.
4. A nap if you can manage one.

Mild shakiness that eases after you eat and drink is a normal part of a rough morning. Shaking that's strong, keeps getting worse, or comes with confusion, a fast heartbeat, or a feeling of dread is different. See the doctor box at the top of this page.

### Home remedies for a hangover upset stomach and heartburn

1. Bland food in small amounts.
2. Water rather than coffee, juice, or carbonated drinks.
3. An over-the-counter antacid can help with heartburn. Follow the label.
4. Don't lie down flat right after eating.

## Natural Hangover Remedies That Don't Hold Up

Some home remedies are popular mainly because they've been passed around for decades. Here's how the common ones actually stack up.

### Hair of the dog (drinking more alcohol)

A drink in the morning can make you feel briefly better because it delays the drop in blood alcohol that drives some hangover symptoms. But it doesn't fix anything. It just pushes the hangover later and adds more for your liver to process. If you find you *need* a morning drink to feel normal, that's worth talking to a doctor about. Full breakdown: [does hair of the dog work](/never-hungover/does-hair-of-the-dog-work).

### A big greasy breakfast

Many people swear by a fry-up. If it makes you feel better, there's no harm in it once your stomach has settled, and the salt and carbs are genuinely helpful. But the grease itself doesn't soak anything up, and heavy fatty food can make nausea and heartburn worse. Eating a proper meal *before* drinking is far more useful than eating one after.

### Pickle juice

Pickle brine is salty, so a small amount does replace some sodium. It's also very acidic, which isn't ideal for a raw stomach. A cup of broth gives you the same salt with less risk of heartburn.

### Raw eggs and "prairie oyster" drinks

Old-school mixtures with raw egg, hot sauce, and Worcestershire carry a small risk of salmonella and offer nothing a cooked egg doesn't. Skip the raw version.

### Sweating it out

A hard workout or a long sauna session makes you lose even more fluid when you're already low. A gentle walk is fine. Intense exercise can wait until tomorrow.

### Orange juice as a cure

Orange juice gives you fluid, sugar, potassium, and vitamin C, which are all fine. It's also acidic and can bother a sensitive stomach. Water it down if you want it. It's a pleasant drink, not a treatment.

## A Simple Home Recovery Routine

If you'd like a plan rather than a list, here's a sensible morning that uses only what most people have in the kitchen.

**When you wake up**

- Drink a glass of water slowly.
- If you're nauseous, have a few crackers or a slice of dry toast and some ginger tea.
- Take your usual coffee if you drink it daily.

**Within the first hour or two**

- Eat a light breakfast: eggs and toast, oatmeal with a banana, or a bowl of broth with rice.
- Keep sipping water or a homemade electrolyte drink.
- If your headache is bad and it's safe for you, take a standard dose of ibuprofen with food.

**Late morning to afternoon**

- Rest or nap.
- Get some fresh air or take a cool shower.
- Eat a proper meal when you're hungry, ideally with protein, vegetables, and some salt.

**That evening**

- Skip alcohol.
- Eat a normal dinner and drink water.
- Go to bed at a reasonable time. You'll usually feel close to normal the next day. If you don't, our guide on [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) explains what's typical and what isn't.

## How This Fits With a Full Hangover Cure Plan

Home remedies are about getting through a bad morning with what you have on hand. If you want the broader picture, including over-the-counter medicines, what the research says about supplements, and how to handle a severe hangover, our [complete hangover cure guide](/never-hungover/how-to-cure-a-hangover-complete-science-guide) is the place to start. For food specifically, see the [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover).

And the most effective remedy of all happens the night before: eating a real meal before you drink, alternating alcohol with water, keeping track of how many drinks you've had, and stopping a couple of hours before bed. Our guide to [preventing a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers those habits.

## Where DHM Fits In

Some people who drink socially add a supplement to the night-before routine. DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree (*Hovenia dulcis*), which has a long history in East Asian folk medicine as a hangover remedy, so in a sense it's a traditional remedy in capsule form. Animal studies suggest it may affect how the body handles alcohol and protect the liver, and a small number of human studies on related outcomes are encouraging, but there is no good evidence yet from large human trials that it prevents hangovers. Treat it as a possible extra, not a replacement for food, water, and pacing yourself.

If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicines, check with a pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best home remedy for a hangover?**

There isn't a single best one, but the combination that helps most people is water with a little salt, a bland carbohydrate like toast or a banana, ginger if you're nauseous, your usual coffee, and rest. None of these cures a hangover. They ease the symptoms while your body recovers, which usually takes several hours to a day.

**How can I get rid of a hangover fast at home?**

You can't make it disappear quickly, but you can feel better faster. Start sipping water right away, eat something bland as soon as you can, use ginger for nausea, take ibuprofen with food for a headache if it's safe for you, and get some sleep. Avoid more alcohol, greasy food on an upset stomach, and extra caffeine.

**What natural remedies help a hangover?**

Water, salty broth, bananas, eggs, toast, ginger, and honey are all reasonable natural options because they replace fluid and salt, settle the stomach, or raise low blood sugar. There is no good evidence that any natural remedy shortens a hangover in a big way. Herbal products sold as hangover cures have mixed and mostly low-quality evidence.

**What should I drink for a hangover at home?**

Water is the first choice. If you've been vomiting or feel very drained, a homemade electrolyte drink (about 4 cups of water, half a teaspoon of salt, and 2 tablespoons of sugar or honey) helps you hold on to fluid. Broth, coconut water, ginger tea, and diluted juice also work. Skip alcohol and go easy on coffee and energy drinks.

**What can I eat to help a hangover?**

Start bland: dry toast, crackers, rice, oatmeal, or a banana. Once your stomach settles, eggs, yogurt, and soup are good choices. Eating doesn't soak up alcohol the next morning, but it raises low blood sugar and gives a sore stomach something gentle to work on.

**Is it safe to take painkillers with home remedies for a hangover?**

Usually, if you choose carefully. Ibuprofen or naproxen taken with food is generally the better option the morning after for healthy adults, though they can irritate the stomach. Avoid acetaminophen (Tylenol) while alcohol is still in your system because the combination is hard on the liver. If you have stomach, kidney, or liver problems, or take other medicines, ask a pharmacist first.

**Does hair of the dog work as a home remedy?**

Not really. Another drink can make you feel better for a short while because it delays the drop in blood alcohol, but the hangover comes back later and your liver has more to process. If you regularly need a morning drink to feel normal, talk to a doctor.

**When should I see a doctor for a hangover?**

Call 911 if someone is confused, can't stay awake, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, or is vomiting while drowsy, since those are signs of alcohol poisoning. See a doctor soon if you can't keep fluids down for most of the day, see blood in vomit or stool, have severe stomach pain or a racing heart that won't settle, or feel worse after 24 hours.
